title: Cues of habitat change and previous success do not modulate songbird breeding‐site fidelity across spatial scales
content:
Our findings highlight a failure of sagebrush songbirds to reduce interannual site fidelity at any spatial scale in response to habitat changes associated with natural gas extraction, which may compound the negative effects of energy development on reproductive success. Reducing initial energy infrastructure footprints and prioritizing habitat restoration following surface disturbance would therefore likely be the most effective management approaches to facilitate nest survival and help forestall further population declines. More generally, taxa that have evolved an ‘always-stay’ site fidelity strategy may be particularly vulnerable to habitat degradation. More explicit incorporation of spatial scales into future assessments of site fidelity would broaden understanding of settlement choices in a changing world.


Abstract

Fidelity to breeding or other sites is a phenomenon that evolved across numerous taxa, yet the scales at which site fidelity operates often are not explicitly evaluated. Moreover, site fidelity that is inflexible can become maladaptive with contemporary habitat change. The cues that animals use when making settlement decisions can vary depending on the ecological context under which fidelity evolved, and the spatiotemporal scales of decision-making. How such decision rules interact with site fidelity in human-altered environments, however, remains unclear. We examined breeding site fidelity in a suite of migratory songbirds (Brewer's sparrow (Spizella breweri), sagebrush sparrow (Artemisiospiza nevadensis) and sage thrasher (Oreoscoptes montanus)) within the North American sagebrush (Artemisia spp.) steppe. We investigated whether site fidelity at three functional spatial scales (landscape, territory and nest-site) varied with breeding-site conditions in the previous year including habitat structure, previous nest success, and a contemporary cue of habitat change that can increase the risk of nest predation (surface disturbance associated with natural gas extraction). Birds largely did not respond to cues in the previous year to inform subsequent site fidelity, with some exceptions. Brewer's sparrows demonstrated higher territory fidelity to disturbed sites, and sagebrush sparrows increased nest-site fidelity based on environmental (lower shrub height) and experiential (previous nest success) cues in the previous year. Synthesis and applications. Our findings highlight a failure of sagebrush songbirds to reduce interannual site fidelity at any spatial scale in response to habitat changes associated with natural gas extraction, which may compound the negative effects of energy development on reproductive success. Reducing initial energy infrastructure footprints and prioritizing habitat restoration following surface disturbance would therefore likely be the most effective management approaches to facilitate nest survival and help forestall further population declines. More generally, taxa that have evolved an ‘always-stay’ site fidelity strategy may be particularly vulnerable to habitat degradation. More explicit incorporation of spatial scales into future assessments of site fidelity would broaden understanding of settlement choices in a changing world.
